# agiter A client-agnostic harness for spec-driven agentic development: you write what you want, cheap models write the drafts, specs, tests and code, other models review them, and the harness keeps every step's input, version, review and decision in files you can read. The design and its reasons are in [docs/design-recap.md](docs/design-recap.md); what changed is in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md). > [!WARNING] > **agiter is alpha software.** Commands, options, file layouts and the formats of its > definitions change often, and any release may break what worked before (the breaking > changes are listed in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md)). At this stage it is meant for studying > agentic development, profiling models and stacks, and proofs of concept, not for the work a > project depends on. Run it in a git repository, review what a run changed before you keep it, > and pin the version you use (`npm install -g @pavel.sommer/agiter@`). Contents: [Install](#install) · [Start a new project](#start-a-new-project) · [Try a sample project](#try-a-sample-project) · [Add agiter to an existing project](#add-agiter-to-an-existing-project) · [Models and agents](#models-and-agents) · [Describe the project](#describe-the-project) · [Workflows](#workflows) · [Costs and usage](#costs-and-usage) · [The stack](#the-stack-presets-blocks-packages) · [Commands](#commands) · [How a run works](#how-a-run-works) · [A run's files](#a-runs-files) · [Layout](#layout) ## The key idea: diverse points of view Every step of a run is done by separate agents, each starting with a fresh context: the author writes, the reviewer judges what was written against the input and the criteria, without the author's reasoning in view, so it has nothing to anchor on and no decision of its own to defend. A next round's author gets its version and the review, not its earlier train of thought. One long prompting session cannot give this: there a model judges its own work with the whole path to it still in context, like a person proofreading what he wrote a minute ago. Context diversity works with the same model too. Model diversity adds a second layer: a model's blind spots come from its training, and a fresh context does not remove them, a different model does. That is why every task has its own model files, one for its author and one for its reviewer: a cheap author and a stronger reviewer of another family make a good pair. ## Install Node.js 22.12 or later (Angular 22 needs 22.22.3), npm 11 or later recommended (npm 10 fails on some packages' peers, Vitest among them), git for isolated runs, and the CLI of at least one agent: [opencode](https://opencode.ai), Claude Code (`claude`), Codex (`codex`), Gemini CLI (`gemini`) or Antigravity CLI (`agy`). ```sh npm install -g @pavel.sommer/agiter agiter --help agiter --help # every command has its options and examples ``` Without a global install, `npx @pavel.sommer/agiter ` does the same. ## Start a new project `agiter new --preset ` makes a new project from a web preset: `agiter/` with the default configuration, the stack, `project.md`, the packages of the stack declared in `package.json`, and the least files that run: an entry page with an App component that shows `

Hello from

`. No sample app, no styles, no tests, no linters. ```sh mkdir shop && cd shop git init # optional; isolated runs need it agiter new # the templates and the presets that make a project agiter new --preset web-react-vite --dry-run # what it would write and run agiter new --preset web-react-vite ``` Nothing is installed yet: look at `package.json` (npm resolved the versions into it and into `package-lock.json`), then install and run: ```sh agiter install # npm install of what package.json declares npm run dev # http://localhost:5173 npm run typecheck npm run build ``` `agiter new --preset web-react-vite --install` does it in one go. The presets with a project: `web-vanilla-javascript`, `web-vanilla-typescript5`, `-6`, `-7` (`web-vanilla-typescript` is 6), `web-react-vite`, `web-react-express`, `web-react-fastify`, `web-react-next`, `web-vue-vite`, `web-vue-nuxt`, `web-svelte-vite`, `web-svelte-kit`, `web-solidjs-vite`, `web-angular`. With `web-react-express` and `web-react-fastify` there is also the API server: `npm run server` beside `npm run dev` (Vite sends `/api` to it; `GET /api/health` answers). `new` overwrites nothing: a file it would write that exists already stops it before anything is written (an existing `.gitignore` is kept). With agiter installed into the folder first (`npm install @pavel.sommer/agiter`, then `npx agiter new …`), the `package.json` npm made gets `"type": "module"`, as the projects are ES modules; one with another type stops `new`. ## Try a sample project A sample preset starts a project with a ready initiative, so you can see a whole run before writing your own. **Notefold** is a local note board in the spirit of Google Keep: a masonry board of notes and checklists, colours and background images with a readable text colour, tags in a resizable side pane, pin, reorder, archive, trash, search, export and import, everything stored in the browser (IndexedDB through Dexie). It comes on four stacks: | Preset | Stack | | --- | --- | | `notefold-web-react-vite` | React + Vite | | `notefold-web-vue-vite` | Vue + Vite | | `notefold-web-solidjs-vite` | SolidJS + Vite | | `notefold-web-vanilla-typescript6` | TypeScript 6, Web Components, Vite, Vitest | ```sh mkdir notefold && cd notefold && git init agiter new --preset notefold-web-react-vite # the project, docs/-notefold.md (Active), agiter/checks.json agiter install git add -A && git commit -m "Notefold, from the sample" agiter run --input docs/-notefold.md --pipeline create-validation # what is still missing (cheap) agiter run --input docs/-notefold.md --pipeline "create-epic create-review:2" # the epics agiter run --isolation worktree --input docs/.epic.E1.md --pipeline "create-draft create-review:2 create-spec create-review:2 create-work create-review checks" ``` `new` prints these steps with the real file names. The initiative is the same on every stack, so it is also a reference input for comparing models and stacks: run it with other models ([Comparing models](#comparing-models)) and compare the runs. A full run to the code is many model calls; mind your limits. ## Add agiter to an existing project ```sh cd my-app agiter init # agiter/ with the default config, project.md, the type notes (spec.md, …) in the root agiter stack --detect # the stack from the project's files (package.json, *.csproj, …) agiter stack --show # what the models will get about the project ``` Or start the stack from a preset, which also declares its packages in `package.json` (through `npm install --package-lock-only`: nothing is installed, so you can look first): ```sh agiter init --preset web-vue-vite # agiter init --help lists every preset agiter install --check # package.json against the blocks: missing, misplaced, another major agiter install --dry-run # what would be installed, the npm commands agiter install # install it ``` `agiter init --preset --install` declares and installs at once. `init` makes no project files; that is `new`. The stack changes later with `agiter stack --add` and `--remove` ([The stack](#the-stack-presets-blocks-packages)). ## Models and agents `agiter init` copies the package's defaults into `agiter/config/`; change them there. `.agents.json` says how to call each agent CLI (`opencode`, `claude`, `codex`, `gemini`, `agy`): its command, how it gets the model, what the reviewer may use, how its JSON output is read. Every agent you use is listed there; an entry may hold only the keys it changes, the rest comes from the package's entry of the same name. Mark an agent you use by subscription, so its calls cost 0 and their API price is kept for comparing: ```json { "opencode": {}, "claude": { "subscription": true }, "codex": { "subscription": true } } ``` A model file names the agent and its models, tried in order until one is available: ```json { "default": { "agent": "opencode", "models": ["openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash"], "select": "availableFirst", "effort": "high", "timeoutMinutes": 30 } } ``` Which file a call uses, the first that exists: | Who | Files | | --- | --- | | the author of task X | `.models.X.json`, `.models.json` | | the reviewer of task X | `.models.X.review.json`, `.models.create-review.json`, `.models.json` | ```sh agiter models --list # which file each task's author and reviewer get ``` A pipeline may name another profile or the agent and model of a step itself (`create-epic@strong`, `claude/claude-opus-5-5/create-epic`): see [Workflows](#workflows). A cheap author with a reviewer of another family: `.models.json` with a flash model, `.models.create-review.json` with `claude`. `create-validation` is a review and has no author, so its own file, `.models.create-validation.json`, is its reviewer's (a cheap one by default); give `create-work` and `create-tests` a good coder. ## Describe the project `agiter/config/project.md` is what every task gets about your project beside the stack: structure, naming, scaffolding, your rules. `agiter init --preset` writes it with the parts its blocks need (the look as CSS custom properties for a browser app, unit tests, browser tests). Its section "Autonomous decisions" sets what the models may decide on their own; by default the effort goes into the functional core of the request, you decide what the user gets and how it behaves and every new dependency, and the look the input does not define is the author's. `agiter/checks.json` lists the checks the `checks` step runs after the work; every one must pass: ```json { "required": [ { "name": "typecheck", "command": "npm run typecheck", "timeoutSeconds": 300 }, { "name": "build", "command": "npm run build", "timeoutSeconds": 600 }, { "name": "test", "command": "npx --no-install vitest run", "timeoutSeconds": 600 } ] } ``` Their output is logged in `agiter/runs//steps/`, one log per check and attempt. ## Workflows The tasks (`agiter list tasks`): | Task | From | Makes | | --- | --- | --- | | `create-initiative` | an idea | an initiative | | `create-validation` | anything | a review of the input as it is: what a working prototype still needs (a report) | | `create-epic` | an initiative | one epic per functional area, and an overview | | `create-draft` | an epic or an idea | a draft | | `create-spec` | a draft or an idea | a spec with its acceptance criteria and its Scope | | `create-tests` | a spec | the tests (before the work, for test-first) | | `create-work` | a spec | the code | | `checks` | anything | the run of `agiter/checks.json` | | `create-profile` | a run | the analysis of a run (`--profile`, `agiter profile`) | A pipeline is a list of tasks, apart by spaces or commas (quote it when it has spaces). A task alone is one round without review; `create-review:N` right after it gives it at most N rounds, each a version and its review (`create-review` alone: one round). First in a pipeline, `create-review` reviews the input once, as it is. A pipeline file (`*.json`) works too, and may hold the run's isolation (`--isolation` is over it); it has no other keys: ```json { "steps": ["create-validation@flash", "create-epic create-review@strong:2"], "isolation": "worktree" } ``` Each token may name the models of its call; the `create-review` token names its reviewer's: | Token | Models | | --- | --- | | `create-epic` | the task's model files, profile `default` (see [Models and agents](#models-and-agents)) | | `create-epic@strong` | the same files, profile `strong`; a run does not start without it | | `claude/create-epic` | the agent with its own default model | | `claude/claude-opus-5-5/create-epic` | the agent and the model; effort and timeout from the `default` profile | | `opencode/openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash/create-epic` | the agent `opencode`, the model `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash` | ```sh agiter run --input --pipeline "create-validation@flash create-epic create-review@strong:2" agiter run --input --pipeline "create-draft create-review:2 create-spec claude/claude-opus-5-5/create-review:2 create-work create-review checks" ``` The first part is always an agent of `.agents.json`. Refused before anything runs: an agent that is not there, an agent/model together with a `@profile`, `:N` on any task but `create-review`, `create-review` after a task without a model author (`create-validation`, `checks`), and the same task twice in a row. ### From an initiative to epics ```sh agiter new initiative --name ocr-inbox # docs/-ocr-inbox.md, status Draft ``` Fill in its "Goal" (the rest is optional), list what you decided already under "Already decided", set `status: Active`, then: ```sh agiter run --input docs/2611151200-ocr-inbox.md --pipeline create-validation # what is still missing agiter run --input docs/2611151200-ocr-inbox.md --pipeline "create-epic create-review:2" --lang cs ``` `create-validation` is cheap and comes before the expensive steps. It reviews the input as it is and writes a report, `docs/.validation.report.md`: what only you can settle (missing, unclear, contradicting) is a blocking finding, what the author can decide alone a minor one, "Left to the author". A blocking finding makes the report Block and stops the run there. Comment the findings in the decisions report (a minor one comes with the comment "Left to the author": leave it or write your own) or edit the input, then run again: every next run on the same file gets your comments. `create-validation,create-epic` does both on the same input, the breakdown only when the validation passed. The epics are published as `docs/.epic.E1.md`, `E2`, … next to an overview. `--lang` sets the language of the output (without it, the language of the input); the headings the harness reads stay in English. ### From an epic or a request to code ```sh agiter run --input docs/2611151300-ocr-inbox.epic.E1.md --pipeline "create-draft create-review:3 create-spec create-review:2 create-work create-review checks" agiter run --text "Add a logout button to the header" --pipeline "create-spec create-review:2 create-work create-review checks" ``` Give the work its review where you can (`create-work create-review`): a work without one is done, not checked. A spec's section "Scope" (`- write:`, `- tests:`, `- protected:` paths) narrows what the work may change. `--includeFile ` (repeatable) gives a file to every model call of the run. Test-first: the tests are written from the spec, then protected from the work: ```sh agiter run --input docs/.spec.md --pipeline "create-tests create-work create-review checks" ``` ### Decisions and open questions Where the input says nothing, the models decide and record it; at the end of the run the decisions are collected into `docs/.decisions.md`. They are for your information: each decision stands as it is, and you need not comment on any. The section "For the owner's information" lists those that change what the user gets or how it behaves; where you want something else, write it in the decision's `Comment:` cell. A run on a document an earlier run wrote gets that run's comments by itself, and they override the document. To have fewer decisions, say more in the input, above all under "Already decided". An open question is different: a run is `blocked` when its last review blocked or the work met an open question (the input contradicts itself, or a criterion cannot be met as written). Its changes go aside as a patch; the question waits in "Open questions of the work" of the decisions report, and its `Answer:` cell must be filled before the work runs again. Whatever stopped a run, you go on with `resume`: ```sh agiter status # the last run: its steps, cost, what blocks it agiter resume # the oldest run that is not done agiter resume notefold # the oldest run notefold (its --id) that is not done agiter resume # that run, by its whole id ``` `resume` shows the run it takes, how it goes on, and asks first; the default is no (`--yes` does not ask, and is needed when the input is not a terminal). Two agiters never work on the same run: a run holds a lock (`agiter/runs//.lock`, who has it) from its start until it stops, and choosing a run to start or resume is one at a time. Run the same command twice by mistake and the second says which agiter has the run (`run --list` shows it as `(running now)`); `resume` without a name leaves it and takes the next one, and `run --delete` never deletes it. When that agiter is gone (a crash, Ctrl+C), its lock is stale and the next one takes it over. Runs side by side work in worktrees. A run in the checkout itself (`--isolation checkout`) or on a branch of it holds the checkout alone: it starts only when no other run works now, and no other run starts while it works (worktree runs publish your documents into the checkout it compares before and after each call). Finishing a run holds the checkout for that while. The records of every run (the calls' prompts, outputs and logs, the checks' logs, the patches) are in `agiter/runs//` of the project, also for a worktree run: they outlast its worktree. Every run's record (`agiter/runs//run.json`) is the harness's state, written whole or not at all. `run`, `plan` and `resume` check all of them first: a record that does not read, or does not say what the harness needs (its status and error, its pipeline and plan, its input, its isolation with a branch and worktree that are there, the calls and models of its steps), stops them with what is wrong and how to go on (fix it, or delete that run). A run its review blocked starts again as a new run: the same pipeline, input, `--id`, `--lang`, `--includeFile` and isolation, another stamp, and your comments in its decisions report (or your changed input). The old run is replaced by it (`run --list` shows `-> `); an isolated one is finished without the merge first. With nothing commented or changed since it stopped, nothing starts. A run that failed, was interrupted or waits for the answers to its open questions goes on where it stopped: nothing done is repeated. ### Accepting Done is not accepted. When a document and what was made from it are what you want: ```sh agiter accept docs/2611151200-ocr-inbox.md ``` It and every document of the runs on it, down the chain, get status `Accepted`, and nothing runs from them any more. ### Isolation: the checkout, a branch or a worktree `--isolation` says where a run works (`agiter isolation --list` lists them): `checkout`, the default, is the current checkout itself, with no commits: you review the changes and commit them. In a git repository it can work apart: ```sh agiter run --isolation checkout --input --pipeline "create-spec create-review:2 create-work create-review checks" # the default agiter run --isolation branch --input --pipeline "create-spec create-review:2 create-work create-review checks" # branch agiter/, a commit per call agiter run --isolation worktree --input --pipeline "create-spec create-review:2 create-work create-review checks" # agiter/.worktrees/; the project's node_modules found up the folders agiter finish --merge # back to the branch it started from, its branch merged (a done run) agiter finish # back without merging ``` What a run gives you in `docs/` (its published documents, the reports, the decisions report, the profile) is always in your checkout, also for a branch or worktree run, and a run never commits it: you read and answer it where you work, it does not make the tree dirty for the next run, and it stays when you finish the run, merged or not. Commit it when you want to keep it. The code and the run's chain (`agiter/docs//`) are on the run's branch. ### Comparing models Name the models in the pipeline, or change the model files between runs without committing them (`agiter/config/.models*.json` and `.agents.json` are yours: a run never commits them), and run the same committed, Active input once per variant, each in its own worktree and named: ```sh agiter run --isolation worktree --id ocr-deepseek --input docs/2611151200-ocr-inbox.md --pipeline "create-spec create-review:2 create-work create-review checks" # edit agiter/config/.models.json … agiter run --isolation worktree --id ocr-opus --input docs/2611151200-ocr-inbox.md --pipeline "create-spec create-review:2 create-work create-review checks" agiter profile # each run's analysis cd agiter/.worktrees/ && npm run dev # try a variant by hand; git checkout agiter/ works too agiter finish --merge # the one you keep; agiter finish for the others ``` A run keeps the models of its start (`run.json`, `models`), so `agiter resume` goes on with them whatever you changed since. `--id` names the run (`-`) and its branch and is part of its identity: an unfinished run of the same input, pipeline and id is resumed, another id is a new run. `--reset` throws the unfinished one away first (its records, documents, links in your input; with isolation its worktree and branch) and starts again. Without isolation, files the old run changed must be restored first (`git restore …`): a reset puts no code back. ### Looking at runs ```sh agiter status [run] # a run (the last one by default): steps, …[仅保留首 16KB/中段 8KB/末 8KB]… urself are yours. Your own packages for the map: `local.packages` in `.stack.json`. ```sh agiter install --dry-run # the packages and the npm commands agiter install # install what package.json lacks, or what it declares and node_modules lacks agiter install --lock-only # only declare them in package.json and package-lock.json agiter install --exact # exact versions instead of ^ ranges agiter install --check # exit 1 when something is missing, misplaced or in another major ``` npm 11.16 and later run a dependency's install scripts only when `package.json` allows them (`allowScripts`; npm 12 blocks the rest). The blocks name the long-trusted packages whose scripts are needed, also those their packages bring (Angular: `esbuild`, `@parcel/watcher`, `lmdb`, `msgpackr-extract`; Nuxt and Vite 6 or 7: `esbuild`; SQLite with better-sqlite3: `better-sqlite3`), and `agiter install` (and `init`, `new`) writes them into `allowScripts` before npm installs, so the scripts run at the install. For packages installed before, it runs `npm rebuild` of them. A package you denied (`false`) stays denied; your own entries: `local.allowScripts` in `.stack.json`. The models never install: the npm block tells them that `package.json` is yours and that a library it does not list is not available, so a work that needs one stops and asks you. Only npm so far; the .NET and LuaJIT blocks have no packages yet. ## Commands | Command | What it does | | --- | --- | | `agiter new --preset [--install] [--dry-run]` | a new project from a web preset: init, the least files that run, the packages declared (or installed) | | `agiter init [--preset ] [--install]` | make a folder an agiter project; with a preset, the stack and its packages declared | | `agiter install [--check \| --dry-run \| --lock-only] [--exact]` | the packages of the stack's blocks | | `agiter isolation --list` | where a run can work: `checkout` (the default), `branch`, `worktree` | | `agiter preset --list` | the presets: which make a project (`[new]`), which a sample (`[sample]`) | | `agiter stack [--list \| --show [role] \| --add … \| --remove … \| --detect]` | the stack's blocks | | `agiter new [--name ] [--title ]` | a new document of yours from a template (initiative, epic) | | `agiter run --pipeline <steps> --input <file> \| --text <text>` | run a scenario (an unfinished run of the same scenario and `--id` is resumed; `--reset` starts it again) | | `agiter plan …`, `agiter simulate … --script <file>` | plan a scenario, run it with a fake model | | `agiter resume [run]` | go on with a run that stopped (default: the oldest that is not done): a new run after a blocking review, the same run after a failure | | `agiter status [run]`, `agiter runs`, `agiter audit [run]` | look at runs | | `agiter profile [run]` | a model analyses a finished run | | `agiter finish [run] [--merge]` | end a branch or worktree run | | `agiter accept <file>` | accept a document and everything made from it | | `agiter models --list` | the model files of each task | | `agiter list tasks \| artifacts` | the definitions | | `agiter sidecar` | the API as JSON-RPC over stdio (for Far Manager) | Exit codes: 0 done (or planned), 1 blocked, failed or invalid, 2 usage. `--json` gives the result as JSON, `--root <dir>` names the project (by default the one the current folder is in). ## How a run works A run's pipeline is always given explicitly. Each step's author and reviewer are separate calls with fresh contexts; a next round's author gets the input, its version and the review. The harness puts into each model's prompt only what its task needs from the stack, then `project.md`, then the decisions made before it. A run that went through is `done`; one whose last review blocked, or whose work stopped on an open question, is `blocked`. A worker without a review decides what the input leaves open, but where the input contradicts itself or a criterion cannot be met as written it does not change the criterion: it names the contradiction under "Open questions", the run stops, its changes go aside as a patch, and the question waits in the decisions report. Tests an earlier `create-tests` wrote are protected from the work. A reviewer that changes a file fails its call (the file is put back); a profile's next model starts from the state before the failed one; a call past its timeout is killed with every process it started. The scope of a step is checked against what git sees. The owner's documents stay his: any file a run did not write is an input in the owner's own form (with a frontmatter `type` it runs only with status `Active`; without one it runs as it is); the pipeline decides what it is (`create-epic`: an initiative), and its frontmatter, status and structure are not checked. A run is named after the input file without its leading timestamp and stamped in local time (`yyMMddHHmmss`); the titles of the outputs are the models' own. A version is Active when another step follows and it has no review or its report is Done; otherwise Draft. A step takes only prose or an Active artifact whose latest report is not Block. The state of a run is its files: `agiter resume` walks the steps again and repeats nothing done. ## A run's files ```text agiter/docs/<run>/.<run>.md the input, copied as it is (never changed; a dot file) agiter/docs/<run>/.<run>.draft.1.md round 1 of create-draft create-review:3 (a dot file) agiter/docs/<run>/.<run>.draft.1.report.md its review: Block or Done, cumulative (a dot file) agiter/docs/<run>/.<run>.draft.2.md round 2: input + draft.1 + its report agiter/docs/<run>/<run>.create-work.1.md the record of create-work docs/<run>.draft.md the result of a step, published docs/<run>.draft.report.md the step's last report, published docs/<run>.decisions.md the decisions report, for the owner to answer docs/<run>.epic.E1.md an epic of create-epic, published ... ``` Two kinds of output. Methodical artifacts (initiative, epic, draft, spec) are the documents a next run builds on: the result of each step (no review, or its report Done) is published to `docs/` (`agiter/config/.settings.json` `{ "docs": "<folder>" }` changes it), never over a file there, and agents never change them. Task records (`create-epic`, `create-work`, `create-tests`, `checks`) and the reports stay in `agiter/docs/<run>/` with every round; the versions of methodical artifacts there are dot files, so a client like Tolaria shows each document once (in `docs/`). Each document's frontmatter has the `model` that wrote it and the `cost` of that call. At the end of a run the file names in its documents become wikilinks (`[[name]]`, as Tolaria resolves them), and the frontmatter gets Tolaria's relationships: `belongs_to` and `related_to`. The owner's input file gets `has` (what runs made from it and keep), `model` (the models they used) and `cost` (their total, over the whole tree that grows from it). Frontmatter types are TitleCase and singular (`Spec`, `Epic`, `Report`, `Decision`); every task's record is `Pipeline`, its `task` tells which. ## Layout | Path | Content | | --- | --- | | `index.mjs` | the public API | | `bin/agiter.mjs` | the CLI on commander (`agiter --help`, `agiter <command> --help`) | | `sidecar.mjs` | JSON-RPC over stdio for long-lived clients (Far Manager) | | `src/` | the modules: definitions, pipelines, artifacts, engine, stack, packages, scaffolds, tools, log | | `defs/` | the package's artifact types, tasks, stack blocks, presets, scaffolds, templates, default config | | `test/` | `npm test` (node:test, no dependencies) | A project keeps everything in `agiter/`: `config/` (agents, models, stack, `project.md`, its own templates in `config/templates/<type>.md` and blocks in `config/blocks/`), `docs/<run>/` (the chain of each run), `runs/`, `logs/`, its own definitions (`artifacts/`, `tasks/`, merged over the package's) and `checks.json` (the required checks).

# Notefold

## Goal

A note board in the spirit of Google Keep that lives entirely in the user's browser: the user
captures, colours, tags, pins, archives and finds short notes and checklists on a masonry
board, with no account and no cloud; everything is stored locally in IndexedDB and survives
reloads, restarts and going offline.

## Users and scenarios

One person on one device, in a desktop browser; notes are personal and short (a thought, a
shopping list, a link, a quote).

1. **First start.** The user opens the app. The board is empty and says so ("Notes you add
   appear here"). The side pane shows Notes (selected), Archive, Trash and an empty Tags
   section with "Edit tags". A gear button in the top bar opens Settings.
2. **Capture a note.** At the top of the board sits a collapsed composer ("Take a note…").
   Clicking it expands it into a Title field and a body field, with a toolbar (colour and
   background, tags, checklist, pin, archive) and a Close button. The user types and clicks
   Close (or clicks outside, or presses Escape). The note appears first in the board. A
   composer closed with an empty title and an empty body adds nothing.
3. **Capture a checklist.** In the composer the user switches to checklist ("New list"). Each
   line is an item with a checkbox; Enter adds the next item, Backspace in an empty item
   removes it. Checking an item moves it to a collapsible "N completed items" group at the
   bottom of the list; unchecking moves it back to the end of the unchecked items. A
   checklist can be turned back into text (one line per item, checked items kept with their
   text).
4. **Edit.** Clicking a card opens it in an editor dialog over the board, the card's place
   kept. Every change is saved as the user types; the dialog shows "Edited <time>". Closing the
   dialog returns focus to the card. "Edited <time>" is relative under a day ("Edited 5 min
   ago"), else a date ("Edited 14 Nov").
5. **Colour and background.** From the palette the user gives a note one of the colours, or a
   background image: one of the 8 images that ship with the app, or one of their own (a file
   picked or dropped onto the editor); "Remove background" takes either away. The text colour of the note follows the background
   (see "Must and must not": contrast), on the card and in the editor.
6. **Tags.** The user creates tags in the side pane ("Edit tags": create, rename, delete) or
   right from a note ("Add tag" with a search field that offers to create the typed tag). A
   note has any number of tags, shown as chips on the card; a chip's × (or unchecking the tag
   in "Add tag") takes that tag off this note only. Clicking a chip, or a tag in the side
   pane, shows only the board's notes with that tag (not the archived or trashed ones), split
   into Pinned and Others like the board; the count beside each tag in the side pane counts
   the same notes.
7. **Pin.** Pinning a note moves it into a "Pinned" section above "Others"; unpinning moves it
   back. Without pinned notes the section headings are not shown.
8. **Reorder.** The user drags a card to another place in its section; the others make room
   as it moves, and the new order is kept.
9. **Archive.** Archiving takes a note off the board into Archive (unpinned). Archive shows
   those notes in the same grid; "Unarchive" puts a note back on the board, first among
   Others.
10. **Delete and restore.** Deleting moves a note to Trash. A toast "Note moved to Trash" offers
    Undo for 5 seconds. Trash says that notes in it are deleted after 7 days, offers "Empty
    Trash" (after a confirmation that says how many notes it deletes), and per note "Restore"
    and "Delete forever" (with a confirmation). Notes in Trash cannot be edited.
11. **Find.** Typing in the search field in the top bar shows, as the user types, the notes
    of the board and the archive whose title, text, checklist items or tags contain the text
    (case- and accent-insensitive), with the matches highlighted, whatever view was selected
    (Notes, a tag, Archive or Trash); the results show the archived ones with an "Archived"
    mark. Clearing the search returns to the view selected before it.
12. **Side pane.** The user drags the pane's edge to make it wider or narrower, or collapses it
    to its icons with the menu button in the top bar. Its width and state are kept across
    reloads.
13. **Several tabs.** With the app open in two tabs, a change in one shows in the other without
    a reload.
14. **Back up and move.** In Settings the user exports everything into one file: every note
    with all its state (on the board, archived or in Trash with when it went there, pinned,
    its position, its times), the tags and the images. Importing such a file, on another
    browser or the same one, adds each note with its state, after the existing notes of its
    section in the file's order; a note whose id is there already is skipped, so importing the
    same file twice adds nothing the second time. A tag of the same name (regardless of case)
    is the existing tag. The app then says "Imported N notes, skipped M already here".

## Must and must not

1. **Local only.** Nothing the user writes or adds ever leaves the device: no request to any
   server at runtime, no analytics, no fonts, images or scripts from a CDN. An open tab keeps
   working with the network off; starting the app with the network off (after a reload) is
   not required.
2. **Never lose an edit.** A change is stored at most 500 ms after the last keystroke, and at
   once when the editor closes or the page is hidden (`pagehide`, `visibilitychange`). A
   failed write is shown to the user (a toast) and retried; it is never dropped silently.
3. **Note.** A note has an id (UUID), a title (up to 1,000 characters), either a text body
   (up to 20,000 characters) or a checklist (up to 500 items of up to 1,000 characters each,
   each item with its own id and checked state), a colour or a background image (the image's
   id and the measured luminance of its text area) or neither, tags (ids), pinned, position,
   created-at, edited-at, archived-at (none when not archived) and deleted-at (none when not in
   Trash). A field at its limit takes no more characters, and a counter shows "<n> / <limit>"
   from 90% of the limit on. Plain text only: no rich text, no Markdown rendering; URLs in the
   text are shown as links that open in a new tab (`rel="noopener noreferrer"`).
4. **Empty notes.** A note whose title and body (or all checklist items) are empty or
   whitespace is not stored; a stored note edited to empty is deleted (to Trash) when its
   editor closes.
5. **Order.** The board shows Pinned, then Others; inside each, the user's order; a new,
   restored or unarchived note goes first in its section. Archive and Trash are ordered by
   archived-at and deleted-at, newest first. The masonry layout fills the columns row by row,
   so the reading order is left to right, then down (not column by column).
6. **Masonry.** Cards are 240 px wide with their own height (content up to a maximum card
   height of 480 px, longer content clipped with a fade); the number of columns follows the
   width of the board; resizing the window or the side pane lays the cards out again
   without a jump of the card under the pointer.
7. **Contrast.** The text of a note keeps a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (WCAG 2.2 AA)
   against what is behind it:
   - on a colour: dark text (#202124) or light text (#FFFFFF), whichever has the higher
     contrast with the colour;
   - on an image: the app measures the image's relative luminance under the text area once,
     when the image is set (on a downscaled copy), stores it in the note, and picks dark or
     light text from it; when neither reaches 4.5:1 (a busy image), it lays a translucent
     scrim (dark under light text, light under dark text) under the text, just strong enough
     to reach 4.5:1;
   - the tag chips, the checkboxes and the toolbar icons of the note follow the same choice.
8. **Images.** A user's image is stored in IndexedDB as a Blob, after downscaling to at most
   1,600 px on the longer side (re-encoded as WebP, or JPEG where WebP encoding is not
   available); files over 20 MB or not an image are refused with a message. An image no note
   uses any more (also after "Delete forever") is deleted from the database.
9. **Tags.** Tag names are unique regardless of case, trimmed, 1 to 50 characters. Renaming a
   tag renames it on every note; renaming it to the name of another tag (regardless of case)
   is refused with "A tag with this name exists" (tags are never merged). Deleting a tag
   removes it from every note (after a confirmation that says how many notes have it). A tag
   view with no notes says so.
10. **Trash.** A note stays in Trash 7 days from when it was deleted; at start, and every hour
    while the app is open, notes older than that are deleted forever. Restore puts a note back
    where it came from (the board or Archive), unpinned.
11. **Data model changes.** The database has a version; every change to its schema comes with a
    Dexie migration that keeps the user's data. An export file has a format version; an import
    is all or nothing: a file of a newer version ("This file is from a newer version of
    Notefold"), or one that breaks the note model (a limit, a missing field, an image no note
    has), is refused with a message and changes nothing.
12. **Multi-tab.** Every view reads the database through live queries (Dexie `liveQuery`), so
    another tab's change appears without a reload; two tabs editing the same note: the last
    write wins, and the open editor shows the newer text when its field is not focused.
13. **Keyboard.** Everything can be done with the keyboard: Tab through the composer, the cards
    and the side pane; Enter opens a card; Escape closes the editor or the composer; `c`
    starts a new note and `/` focuses the search when no field is focused; dragging a card
    has a keyboard alternative ("Move up", "Move down" in the note's menu).
14. **Must never:** block the board while images load (a card shows its colour or a neutral
    placeholder until its image is decoded); show another note's content in the editor after
    a fast switch; leave a dialog open with the focus behind it.

## Constraints

1. A single-page application in the browser; no backend, no service worker beyond what the
   stack's build gives (offline after load is enough; installing as a PWA is out of scope).
2. The stack is the project's (its preset); the code follows the stack's rules.
3. Storage: IndexedDB through Dexie 4 (`dexie`), with `liveQuery` for every view. This is the
   only runtime dependency the initiative adds to the stack; anything else (a masonry, drag
   and drop or UI library) is the owner's decision and needs his approval first.
4. Masonry, drag and drop, the resizable pane and the contrast computation are the app's own
   code (CSS and the platform: CSS Grid or absolute positioning, Pointer Events,
   `ResizeObserver`, Canvas or `createImageBitmap` for the luminance).
5. Browser: the current stable Google Chrome on the desktop, as the stack's browser block says.
   Phones and touch are out of scope (the layout must not break on a narrow window, nothing
   more).
6. The 8 background images that ship with the app are drawn for it as SVG files in the
   project (abstract shapes, paper textures, light gradients; the author draws them, nothing
   is taken from elsewhere), each at most 50 KB, licensed with the project.

## Look

1. Close to Google Keep's light theme: a top bar (menu button, app name "Notefold", the search
   field in the middle, the view settings on the right), the side pane on the left, the
   composer centred above the board.
2. The side pane: icon and label per item (Notes, Tags…, Archive, Trash), the selected item
   highlighted with a rounded background; 280 px wide by default, resizable between 200 and
   400 px by a 4 px handle on its right edge (cursor `col-resize`), collapsed to 72 px (icons
   only).
3. Cards: 240 px wide, 8 px corner radius, 1 px border (#E0E0E0) on white, 16 px gap; the
   toolbar of a card appears on hover or focus; a pinned card shows the pin icon.
4. The colour palette (light theme), as CSS custom properties: Default #FFFFFF, Coral
   #FAAFA8, Peach #F39F76, Sand #FFF8B8, Mint #E2F6D3, Sage #B4DDD3, Fog #D4E4ED, Storm
   #AECCDC, Dusk #D3BFDB, Blossom #F6E2DD, Clay #E9E3D4, Chalk #EFEFF1.
5. The editor dialog: up to 600 px wide, the note's colour or image as its background, the
   toolbar at the bottom, "Edited <time>" at the bottom right, the board dimmed behind it.
6. A system font stack (no web fonts); icons as inline SVG (no icon font from a CDN).

## Out of scope

Accounts, sync, sharing and collaborators; reminders and notifications; drawings, voice notes
and image attachments inside the text (an image is only a background); rich text and Markdown
rendering; a list view of the board; a dark theme; multi-select and bulk actions; mobile and
touch layouts; installing as a PWA; languages other than English in the UI.

## Quality bar

A reference project, kept and extended later; also the reference input for comparing models,
so its result must be checkable:

1. Unit tests for the data layer (notes, tags, positions, trash purge, export and import, the
   schema migrations on an IndexedDB fake), for the contrast choice (colours, and the scrim
   from a given luminance) and for the masonry placement (positions from card heights and a
   width).
2. Browser acceptance tests for the scenarios 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 14 of "Users and
   scenarios", against the dev server, on a fresh database each.
3. Measured by a browser test on the production build (`vite preview`), with 1,000 notes the
   test seeds: within 1,000 ms of the navigation every card is placed and the search field
   answers a typed character; while the test scrolls the board and drags a card, no long task
   over 50 ms (`PerformanceObserver`, `longtask`). The test records its numbers and the
   machine it ran on.
4. Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 AA for the app's own UI: names for every control, the dialog as a
   modal dialog with focus kept inside and returned, visible focus, the contrast rule above
   also for the app's chrome.
5. No error or warning in the browser console during the acceptance tests.

## Already decided

- The UI says "Tags", not "Labels".
- Deleting is soft: Trash for 7 days, as in Google Keep.
- Text colour is dark #202124 or light #FFFFFF, picked by contrast; a scrim only when neither reaches 4.5:1.
- User images are downscaled to 1,600 px and stored as Blobs in IndexedDB, never as data URLs in the note.
- Note ids are UUIDs (`crypto.randomUUID()`); times are stored as epoch milliseconds (UTC).
- Positions are fractional (a number between the neighbours), so a move writes one note only.
- Search is client-side over all notes on the board and in the archive, not in Trash.
- The export is one JSON file (images as base64), format version 1, named `notefold-<yyyy-MM-dd>.json`.
- No dark theme in this initiative.
- A tag view shows the board's notes only; search always covers the board and the archive.
- An import keeps each note's id and skips the ids already there; it never merges or overwrites a note.
- Only the current stable Google Chrome is targeted.
